latest.title: Solar is mainstream power. What does that mean for the energy industry’s future?
latest.notes: Howard Wenger, president of Nextpower, first got interested in solar power during the energy crisis of the 1970s. In his 42-year career in the industry, he has seen an astonishing transformation, as solar has moved from a niche technology for highly specialized applications to a core contributor to meeting electricity demand. In this special episode of Energy Gang from the RE+ conference in Las Vegas, he talks to host Ed Crooks about where the solar industry is now, and where it is going in the future. Nextpower is a company that provides systems for the solar and storage industries, including trackers, inverters, foundations and electrical balance of system. As Howard says, “everything but the panel for large scale solar power and everything but the battery cell for battery storage.” It is a big player in the industry, providing equipment for 30% of all the power installed in the US last year. The AI data-center buildout is pushing electricity demand sharply higher, often faster than utilities can deliver grid connections. That creates demand for behind-the-meter power, often as an interim step until a grid connection can be agreed, and solar and storage have a vital role to play. Howard says the debate is often not about solar and storage versus gas, but about how solar and storage and gas can be combined to provide the cleanest possible power as quickly as possible, with the availability and reliability that data center operators demand. Howard’s argument is that by combining trackers, inverters, foundations, wiring and software into an engineered package, Nextpower can reduce costs, raise output, speed construction and lower project risk. Charged up by rising electricity demand, the business is growing fast. In its capital markets day for investors, held shortly before Howard spoke to Ed, the company raised its target for 2030 revenues by almost 50%, from $5.2 billion to $7.5 billion. The discussion also goes into the impact of policy uncertainty on solar and storage. With the successes for Democrats in the US midterm elections, speculation has inevitably been on the rise about possible future expansions and extensions of tax credits for renewable energy. But not everyone in the industry is enthusiastic about that prospect. Howard says Nextpower would be comfortable without clean-energy incentives, if the playing field with fossil fuels were level. However, he adds, the import tariffs and other additional costs placed on solar and storage mean that continued support from tax credits is needed. Nextpower™ (Nasdaq: NXT) is addressing that complexity by bringing together solar power generation, energy storage, power conversion, data intelligence and lifecycle services in one integrated technology platform. Building on more than a decade of leadership in utility-scale solar tracking, Nextpower engineers, delivers and supports technologies that help developers, utilities, and asset owners build faster, generate more energy and reduce long-term risk. latest.title: Ethan Zindler and Lily Bermel on Clean Energy's Headwinds and Tailwinds
latest.notes: Earlier this month, US voters handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress and flipped several governorships across the country. The dramatic shift in power raises big questions about where US energy policy is headed. Following the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act—which ended or cut back many of the Inflation Reduction Act's clean energy tax credits—analysts warned that new clean power additions could fall by more than half over the next decade. But the buildout has held up better than many expected. Last year, the US added more new power capacity than it had in over two decades, most of it coming from clean energy sources. Rising electricity demand, much of it from data centers, keeps pushing developers to build. Recent analyses suggest the clean energy buildout will keep growing, even without the full set of tax incentives. So what does the incoming Congress mean for clean energy policy? Should Democrats spend their political capital on restoring the tax credits or on clearing bottlenecks like permitting? With hyperscalers heavily relying on new natural gas capacity, how can policymakers make the case for clean energy heading into 2028? Today on the show, Jason Bordoff talks to Ethan Zindler and Lily Bermel about how Trump administration policies have impacted the state of clean energy in the US. Ethan Zindler is a non-resident fellow at the Center on Global Energy Policy (CGEP) and leads country and policy research at BloombergNEF (BNEF). Lily Bermel is a visiting fellow at CGEP and also consults with climate philanthropies on clean industrial strategy. Credits: Hosted by Jason Bordoff, Bill Loveless, and Daniel Sternoff. latest.title: [Episode #287] – Clearing the Connection Queue
latest.notes: Around the world, renewable energy and storage projects are waiting years in queues before they can come onto the grid. Even as the energy transition accelerated, many of these queues continued to run on the conventional first-come, first-served basis. So speculative proposals could get ahead of projects that were practical to build, providing a headwind on how fast the transition could move. Britain is one example, where in December 2025, its National Energy System Operator (NESO) told a committee of Parliament that 70% of the projects in its queue would never be built. Nine months later, Britain’s Minister for Energy told another committee that the connection dates many projects had been holding were “a work of fiction in most cases.” What would it take to get real projects onto the grid faster, so that they can cut carbon emissions and make our energy supply more sustainable? A version of that question is under debate in the US as this episode is released. Congress is considering a wide-ranging bill on permitting and the power grid, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which, among other changes, would reform interconnection queues to discourage speculative projects. In this episode of our documentary series, we look at the reforms and proposals in Britain, the US, Europe and Australia for getting projects through these queues faster and building the power lines they need, drawing on public recordings and episodes featuring conversations with our host Chris Nelder. We’ll hear why, nearly a decade ago, a state utility commission could tell a company that wanted to build a multi-state power line that it couldn’t even apply for a permit, because it had no customers in that state. And we’ll hear about tenants in the German city of Neumünster who have spent two years looking at the solar panels on the roofs of their buildings, still waiting for the local grid operator to connect them. latest.title: Enter the electric supercycle [re-published]
latest.notes: Note: In observation of Thanksgiving, this week we are re-publishing one of our favorite episodes of 2026. Look out for a new episode of Catalyst next week. /// While many energy insiders remain focused on the staggering demand coming from AI and data centers, a much larger and far-reaching shift is happening. We are entering what Energy Impact Partners’ head of research Andy Lubershane calls the "electric supercycle" — a series of interlocking technological flywheels that are accelerating the clean energy transition faster than many may realize. In this episode, Shayle sits down with Andy to map out the interconnected nature of the "electric stack.” They unpack how early investments in solar and EVs are scaling up technologies that are now feeding back into grid infrastructure, and look ahead to the massive electricity demands of the coming robotics and defense industry boom. They also consider the pressing question of the ultimate rate limiters for meeting this demand. Shayle and Andy discuss topics like: - The power grid supply crunch - Why electricity prices have tracked inflation so far, but may surge past it when equipment costs hit retail customer bills. - The four pillars of the electroindustrial tech stack: Solar PV, lithium-ion batteries, EVs, and wide-bandgap power electronics - How a "Robo-Butler" load profile compares to other household appliances - How the defense industry could catalyze climate tech, especially batteries - Why physical transmission corridors remain the top rate limiter for the energy transition - ⁠ Andy Lubershane’s Substack post, “Riding the Electric Supercycle” ⁠ - ⁠ Catalyst: ⁠ Five big questions about the future of energy (with Andy Lubershane) - ⁠ Catalyst ⁠ : Surprising trends in global electricity generation - ⁠ Catalyst ⁠ : Live from Transition-AI 2026: Inside Google’s massive AI capex - ⁠ Catalyst ⁠ : AI scaling pathways: On grid, on edge, off grid, off planet - ⁠ Open Circuit ⁠ : America’s electricity rage is here - ⁠ Open Circuit ⁠ : Have we run out of big ideas to fix the grid? latest.title: Data centers need to earn their power [partner content]
latest.notes: Data center developers face a difficult choice: wait years for a traditional grid connection, or build their own power systems and operate independently of the grid. But a third path is emerging. By bringing onsite generation, batteries, and sophisticated software controls, data centers can be more flexible when the grid is constrained — and potentially connect to the system faster. But batteries alone don't make a data center flexible. They need to be coordinated in real time to meet the demands of the facility, the utility, and the broader electricity market. And the stakes go well beyond the data center industry. If these new loads can help utilities avoid expensive infrastructure upgrades, they could also help limit electricity bill increases for a wider range of consumers. In this partner episode, produced in collaboration with Verse, Stephen Lacey talks with Seyed Madaeni, co-founder and CEO of Verse. They talk about the growing role of flexibility in connecting data centers. How do we ensure the rush to power AI allows us to build a more distributed, resilient, and affordable electricity system? This episode was produced in partnership with Verse. Verse helps large energy buyers secure power faster and manage electricity costs through intelligent software that optimizes energy procurement, batteries, and onsite power assets. Learn how Verse is helping data centers unlock faster grid connections through flexibility.

latest.title: Clean firm power’s next test: Can nuclear and geothermal scale economically?
latest.notes: Rising electricity demand, especially from AI and data centers, has brought nuclear and geothermal back into focus as sources of clean, firm power. But demand, corporate partnerships and policy support are not the same as projects delivering affordable electricity on time. The central question is whether both technologies can turn renewed momentum into repeatable deployment. Host Caitlin Connolly, Senior Analyst at Wood Mackenzie, is joined by Jenifer Shafer, professor of chemistry and Ben L. Fryrear Presidential Chair at Colorado School of Mines, and Anna Littlefield, Geothermal and Low Carbon Technologies Program Manager at the Payne Institute for Public Policy. They compare what is driving this moment and where the routes to scale diverge. On nuclear, uprates and restarts could add capacity sooner than new builds, while small modular reactors are more likely to arrive in the 2030s. Shafer explains how fuel recycling could improve fuel security and reduce the amount of material requiring disposal, but would not remove the need for a repository. Cost, safeguards and social license remain central challenges, while progress through the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is a key signal to watch. Enhanced geothermal systems aim to reach heat in deep rock beyond the limited areas served by conventional hydrothermal resources. Drilling and reservoir engineering have advanced, but the test now is whether projects can sustain heat flow economically over time while managing water loss, scaling, corrosion and reservoir performance. Littlefield points to power purchase agreements scheduled for the 2028 to 2030 period as an important test of delivery, not yet proof of scale. Colorado’s permitting and development efforts, including work to assess whether treated oil and gas produced water can support geothermal circulation, may offer lessons for other states. The technologies face different constraints: nuclear must address fuel, waste and project execution, while geothermal must prove durable reservoirs and manage water and induced-seismicity concerns. Both also depend on community trust. The guests argue that developers need to listen to local concerns and share monitoring data, rather than assume technical explanations alone will win support. Over the next five years, the clearest evidence will be projects that reach operation and perform as promised, alongside nuclear licensing progress and geothermal’s ability to deliver contracted power reliably. latest.title: 256. Survival of the Fittest: The New Rules of Renewable Investing - Nov26
latest.notes: The renewable energy landscape has changed dramatically over the past decade. In the 2010s, investors benefited from cheap financing, generous government support and power grids able to absorb renewable intermittency. Today, the industry faces curtailment, negative power prices, declining capture rates, the end of subsidy schemes and significantly higher interest rates. So how do you survive – and thrive – as a renewable energy investor in this new environment? While some players are facing financial distress, others have successfully adapted and are thriving. In this episode, Laurent and Gerard sit down with Jordi Francesch, Global Head Clean Energy at Nuveen Infrastructure. Nuveen, the asset management subsidiary of TIAA, oversees approximately $2.6 trillion in public and private assets. Its renewable energy platform brings together Glennmont Partners, acquired in 2021, and Greencoat, acquired through Schroders in 2026. Combined, they represent more than 20 GW of wind, solar and battery storage assets, potentially positioning Nuveen as a major player in the consolidation wave ahead. Jordi explains how the market has evolved and how Nuveen has adapted its investment and asset management strategies. We discuss power shaping, portfolio management, hedging and trading, as well as emerging opportunities across technologies and geographies. We also explore how banks have changed their approach to financing renewable assets and, finally, how AI is transforming the way these assets are procured, financed and managed. The renewable investment playbook has changed. This conversation is about understanding the new rules and learning how to thrive in the next chapter of the energy transition. Welcome to the Jungle: Are you a prey or a predator?

latest.title: Yardstick: What Climate Tech Founders Need to Know About Venture Capital
latest.notes: Raising venture capital is often presented as a series of milestones: find investors, close a seed round, raise a Series A, and keep scaling. But what happens when a company does all those things successfully—and yet the market was built for changes? Chris Tolles, co-founder & CEO of Yardstick, joins Climate Rising to reflect on building and financing a soil carbon measurement company from its founding in 2020 through its decision to end commercial operations in 2026. Yardstick successfully developed a technology to measure carbon content in agricultural soils, raised multiple venture rounds, attracted investors including corporate, climate, and conservation-focused capital, and secured significant U.S. government contracts. However, in 2025 roughly $20 million of Yardstick’s USDA contracts were canceled. Chris was faced with tough decisions about how the company should move forward, and what to do with the potentially climate critical technology they had developed. Chris discusses how government funding helped de-risk Yardstick’s earliest venture financing, what fundraising labels such as pre-seed and Series A actually mean, how founders should evaluate investors beyond the money they provide, and why investor relationships and alignment become especially important when companies face difficult decisions. The conversation also explores a fundamental tension in climate entrepreneurship: venture capital moves quickly, while natural systems—and the markets built around them—often do not.

latest.title: What the World Fears of a Lame-Duck Trump: A Conversation With Daniel W. Drezner and Elizabeth N. Saunders
latest.notes: Donald Trump’s second-term foreign policy has brought some continuity, with the president acting on long-standing fixations on trade and allies and more. It’s also brought some surprises, especially when it comes to the use of military force. Now, Trump is entering the lame-duck period of his presidency. And with larger-than-expected midterm wins, Democrats are making grand promises about ending the war in Iran, exposing globe-spanning corruption, and much else. In a recent article for Foreign Affairs , Daniel Drezner, a professor of international politics at Tufts, and Elizabeth Saunders, a professor of political science at Columbia, considered what Trump can, and cannot, achieve internationally in the next two years. Dan Kurtz-Phelan spoke with them on Wednesday, November 18, about the possible consequences of Trump’s lame-duck foreign policy—and about the debates within both parties about what should come next. You can find sources, transcripts, and more episodes of The Foreign Affairs Interview at https://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/foreign-affairs-interview.

latest.notes: This episode unpacks what the 2026 midterm elections mean for Congress, bipartisanship, and the future of U.S. foreign policy. Host: James M. Lindsay , Mary and David Boies Distinguished Senior Fellow in U.S. Foreign Policy, CFR Guest: Will Hurd , former U.S. representative from Texas and president of ICON Prime We Discuss: What Will Hurd's own survival of the 2018 blue wave—winning by 920 votes while forty-one Republican colleagues lost—reveals about who ends up holding the most vulnerable seats. Whether a chastened Republican Party will break with President Trump after the midterms, or close ranks to avoid 2028 primary challenges. Whether Congress can reclaim its oversight role, particularly in an age of artificial intelligence. Where Republicans and Democrats might still cooperate in the next Congress, including on legal immigration, Ukraine, tariffs, and rebuilding the U.S. military footprint in the Middle East. latest.title: Middle Powers Unite at the Halifax International Security Forum
latest.notes: One of the big questions on my mind heading into this year's Halifax International Security Forum in Nova Scotia was how the Democratic landslide in the midterm elections would shape discussions among leading security officials from Canada, the United States, and Europe. On the one hand, the forum once again lacks participation from senior American officials. Despite the presence of a bipartisan U.S. Senate delegation, no State Department or Pentagon officials are attending—a deliberate choice by the Trump administration. On the other hand, the Democrats' strong showing in the midterms could have sent a message to middle powers that Trump's political dominance is not necessarily enduring. So, are they preparing for the United States to return to a common security architecture, or are they following Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's lead and declaring the Trump era a "rupture" from which the world cannot return? Joining me for this special live edition of Global Dispatches is Justin Ling, a columnist for the Toronto Star and proprietor of the Bug-Eyed and Shameless Substack. We discuss the state of U.S.-Canada relations, the prospects for middle-power diplomacy, and other highlights from this year's Halifax International Security Forum.
